titre: The Smoke That Crossed a Border and Created a Rule
accroche: As early as 1925, the fumes from a Canadian smelter scorch American fields. A tribunal's response, in 1941, still underpins environmental law.
contenu_vulgarise:
At Trail, British Columbia, about twelve kilometers as the crow flies from the American border, the lead and zinc smelter of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company grows during the 1920s. In 1925 and 1927, two new smokestacks are built there. Carried by the wind, their sulfur dioxide-laden fumes cross the border and fall on the farms of Washington State. As early as 1925, crops wither, trees yellow, soils turn acidic.

American farmers file complaints. In 1935, with no amicable settlement, Canada and the United States sign a convention creating a special arbitral tribunal to settle the dispute.

## A Rule Laid Down After Sixteen Years of Inquiry

The tribunal issues a first award in 1938, which sets damages for the period from 1932 to 1937 at $78,000, then resumes its inquiry to rule on the future: must the smelter keep emitting, and on what conditions? Its final award, issued on March 11, 1941, answers with a principle that goes far beyond the case at hand. No state, the tribunal writes, has the right to use or permit the use of its territory in such a manner as to cause injury by fumes in or to the territory of another state, when the case is of serious consequence and the injury is established by clear and convincing evidence.

The tribunal does not stop at a figure for compensation, as the Alabama tribunal had done in 1872 for harm already caused. It sets an operating regime for the future, with emission thresholds measured hour by hour, to keep the pollution from starting again. It is this preventive dimension, a law that governs an activity for the future rather than merely repairing a past wrong, that makes Trail Smelter last.

## A Principle That Became the Basis of Environmental Law

What Trail Smelter announces is the idea that a state remains responsible for what leaves its territory, even when the cause is a private factory and not an act of the state itself. Pollution does not stop at political borders, but legal responsibility still does, and someone must answer for it.

The principle laid down in 1941 is taken up thirty-one years later in the 1972 Stockholm Declaration on the environment, which states in very similar terms that states have the obligation to ensure that activities carried out on their territory do not cause damage to the environment of other states. A lead and zinc smelter lost in a valley in British Columbia thus supplied, unintentionally, the founding formula of an entire branch of international law.

citation.texte: no State has the right to use or permit the use of its territory in such a manner as to cause injury by fumes in or to the territory of another or the properties or persons therein, when the case is of serious consequence and the injury is established by clear and convincing evidence
citation.source: Trail Smelter case (United States v. Canada), award of March 11, 1941, Reports of International Arbitral Awards, vol. III, p. 1965

carte.punch: Smoke that crossed a border ended up founding environmental law.
carte.idee: As early as 1925, a Canadian smelter pollutes American farms across the border. In 1941, an arbitral tribunal lays down a principle still cited today: no state has the right to use its territory in such a way as to cause serious harm to the territory of another state.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Full text of the awards (Reports of International Arbitral Awards, vol. III)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The final award of March 11, 1941 also details the regime of emission thresholds imposed on the smelter for the future.

quiz.question: How does the 1941 award on the Trail smelter go further than a mere order to repair damage already done?
choix: It transfers ownership of the smelter to an international body responsible for monitoring it
It permanently bans all industrial activity within fifteen kilometers of the border
It sets emission thresholds for the future, laying down a principle of territorial responsibility that goes beyond the dispute decided
It annuls the 1935 Ottawa convention to replace it with a permanent bilateral treaty
quiz.explication: The tribunal does not stop at putting a figure on the damage already suffered: it imposes measurable emission thresholds to keep the pollution from resuming, and it states a general principle of a state's responsibility for what leaves its territory, since taken up in international environmental law.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where was the smelter in question located, and how far from the American border?
choix: In Vancouver, more than two hundred kilometers from the American border
In Trail, but directly on the border line between the two countries
In Washington State, on the American side of the border
In Trail, British Columbia, about twelve kilometers from the border
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The smelter is at Trail, British Columbia, about twelve kilometers as the crow flies from the American border, from where its fumes reached the farms of Washington State.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the $78,000 compensation set by the 1938 award cover?
choix: All damage since the smokestacks were built in 1925
Future damage, estimated for the ten years following the award
Damage occurring between January 1, 1932 and October 1, 1937
The legal costs incurred by the American farmers to bring their complaint
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first award, issued in 1938, sets damages at $78,000 for the damage occurring between January 1, 1932 and October 1, 1937, not for the damage since the pollution began.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened thirty-one years after the final 1941 award, according to the entry?
choix: The International Court of Justice annuls the award for a procedural defect
The 1972 Stockholm Declaration takes up a very similar principle on states' territorial responsibility
Canada pays new compensation, ten times greater than in 1938
The Trail smelter is permanently closed on the tribunal's order
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The principle laid down in 1941 is taken up thirty-one years later in the 1972 Stockholm Declaration, which states in similar terms the obligation of states for damage originating from their territory.
